questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching an actor category to what it wants
questions.learningObjective: Identify what each actor category is actually optimising for
questions.stem: The design brief's threat model lists four actor categories; which pairing states what each one is actually optimising for?

options.text: State-aligned campaign: maximise public attention and recruitment for its political cause
options.misconception: conflates a political goal with the operational payoff

options.text: Organised crime crew: secure a single lucrative heist and then disband the group
options.misconception: treats crime as a one-off job rather than a business

options.text: Espionage actor: hold quiet access inside the target for as long as the intelligence need lasts
Activist crew: maximise operational tempo to flood the news cycle within one week
options.misconception: reads attention-seeking as the activist's true objective

questions.explanation: An espionage actor's payoff is durable access and steady collection, not publicity or a single score. The other options misread motive: crime as one-off work, activism as pure news volume.
questions.hint: Ask what each actor keeps, not what they announce.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a state-aligned campaign tolerates a long stay inside
questions.learningObjective: Explain why long dwell time fits a state-aligned campaign
questions.stem: The design brief describes an intrusion that stayed dormant for eleven months inside a research network; which reading of that dwell time fits the brief's reasoning?

options.text: The operator kept access because the intelligence objective could not be obtained in one short visit
The operator lacked the skill to complete the objective during the initial compromise
options.misconception: treats dwell time as evidence of incompetence

options.text: The operator was waiting for a contractual renewal window before acting on the data
options.misconception: reads a calendar coincidence as attacker intent

options.text: The operator maintained the channel so the target's staff would not notice a sudden outage
options.misconception: confuses availability protection with intelligence goals

questions.explanation: Long dwell fits a campaign needing sustained access a one-shot intrusion cannot deliver. The other readings explain the delay through incompetence or coincidence rather than deliberate collection.
questions.hint: Ask what the extra weeks bought the operator.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes criminal operations a business
questions.learningObjective: Explain the features that make criminal intrusion a business
questions.stem: The design brief argues that criminal intrusion crews operate like small businesses; explain the three features that make that framing more than a slogan.

answer.exemplar: Three features support the business framing. First, revenue is recurring rather than one-off, so access to payment systems is retained and monetised repeatedly. Second, the work is divided into roles, with reconnaissance, access and cash-out handled by different people. Third, the crew invests in tooling and repays access brokers, treating the operation as a revenue stream that must stay profitable.

questions.explanation: Recurring revenue, divided roles and reinvestment in tooling are what make the business framing more than a label. Treating the crew as a one-off heist misses the repeat monetisation.
questions.hint: Look for repeat revenue and division of labour.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an activist campaign is optimising for
questions.learningObjective: Compute the audience an activist event generates
questions.stem: The design brief estimates that 840 people will attend an action directly and that each brings 1.2 guests; how many guest attendees does the brief expect in total?
questions.explanation: Guests equal attendees times guests each: 840 times 1.2 gives 1008. Assuming one guest each gives 840, and reading 1.2 as the whole guest total would give a number far below the plan.
questions.hint: Multiply headcount by guests per person.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The asymmetry an insider holds
questions.learningObjective: Characterise the advantage an insider holds over defenders
questions.stem: The design brief warns about insider risk; which statement captures the asymmetry an insider actually holds against the defenders?

options.text: The insider already holds valid credentials, so any access they use is indistinguishable from legitimate use
options.misconception: assumes valid credentials erase all traceability

options.text: The insider can change files without leaving traces, because insiders write through the normal application path
options.misconception: believes normal write paths create no audit records

options.text: The insider knows which monitoring tools are deployed and can therefore avoid the paths that are logged
options.misconception: assumes knowing the tools removes the logging

options.text: The insider sees intent and context that log records never capture, so misuse can look like ordinary work

questions.explanation: The insider's real advantage is context: they know what normal work looks like and can dress misuse as routine. Valid credentials extend the cover, and knowing which tools exist does not delete what they record.
questions.hint: Think about what a log never records.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a supply-chain compromise travels so far
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a supply-chain compromise multiplies its reach
questions.stem: A design brief considers a compromised build dependency that reaches 400 downstream services; which two-part explanation best accounts for the distance the compromise travels?

options.text: It is signed by the vendor, so every consumer trusts the artefact and installs it without review
options.misconception: assumes signing removes the need for review

options.text: It is trusted implicitly at build time, and each downstream service re-distributes it onward, multiplying reach
It waits for a network partition so the updater retries later against an unpatched mirror
options.misconception: invents a network partition as the mechanism

options.text: It replaces the package registry entry so every install in the organisation pulls it
options.misconception: confuses the affected path with the general one

questions.explanation: Reach comes from implicit trust at build time plus re-distribution, so each consumer becomes the next distributor. Signing proves origin rather than safety, and the registry path is narrower than the one described.
questions.hint: Trust at build time, then onward sharing.

options.text: The site exposes the internal addressing plan because subdomains are listed in the staff directory
options.misconception: assumes a staff page lists internal addresses

options.text: The site reveals staff names, roles and vendor pages that let an attacker target plausible people and suppliers
The site contains the recovery codes for the backup account because they were pasted into a status page
options.misconception: invents a disclosure of recovery codes

options.text: The site is the only place where administrator accounts can be created, so the attacker simply signs up
options.misconception: assumes public self-service creates admin accounts

questions.explanation: A public site tells an attacker who and what to aim at: named staff, their roles, the suppliers they rely on. The other options invent disclosures the brief never records, including recovery codes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The dilemma a zero-day finder faces
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the trade-off in disclosure timing
questions.stem: The design brief compares a researcher who disclosed a flaw privately after 30 days with one who published on day 3; which statement best reflects what the brief concludes?

options.text: Publishing on day 3 was clearly correct because every vendor ignores private reports
options.misconception: generalises one vendor's behaviour into a rule

options.text: Disclosure after 30 days was clearly wrong because private channels leak to competitors
options.misconception: assumes confidential channels leak by default

options.text: Both routes protect users equally, so the timing of disclosure does not matter
options.misconception: denies any difference without evidence

options.text: Timing trades off vendor fix time against user exposure, so neither route is automatically correct

questions.explanation: The brief treats timing as a trade-off between the vendor's patch window and user exposure. Calling either route automatically right or wrong ignores how fast the vendor can genuinely ship a fix.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching an actor category to what it wants
questions.learningObjective: Compare what cash-seeking and leverage-seeking actors optimise
questions.stem: The design brief asks why an actor who only wants cash behaves differently from an actor who wants leverage; explain what each is optimising for and how that shapes their choices.

answer.exemplar: The cash-seeking actor optimises for the largest immediate, repeatable extraction and avoids attention that would interrupt the revenue stream, so speed of collection and a quiet exit matter most. The leverage-seeking actor optimises for change in the target's decisions, so it values publicity, a visible record and continued access. That difference explains why one hides its tracks and the other deliberately leaves evidence.

questions.explanation: Cash is maximised by fast repeatable extraction and low visibility; leverage is maximised by visibility, evidence and continued access. Those two axes explain why the categories behave differently.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate dwell time needed to reach a collection goal
questions.stem: The design brief models a resident operator that retrieves 4 documents per week against a collection goal of 260 documents; after how many weeks of dwell is that goal met?
questions.explanation: Weeks needed is the goal divided by the weekly rate: 260 over 4 gives 65 weeks. Reading the rate as monthly, or converting to months before dividing, gives a misleading dwell figure.
questions.hint: Divide the goal by the weekly rate.

questions.topic: What makes criminal operations a business
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish business operations from one-shot theft

stimulus.body: Operator A rents access to a shipping portal for a month, uses it to invoice customers, and pays the broker per successful login. Operator B buys one set of harvested credentials, uses them the same afternoon, and does not renew.

questions.stem: The design brief quotes an operator comparison; which reading best fits the brief's argument that criminal operations behave like businesses?

options.text: Operator B is the better-run operation because finishing the job in one session proves superior efficiency
options.misconception: reads one-shot speed as operational maturity

options.text: Neither operator is a business because both rely on someone else for initial access
options.misconception: dismisses rented access as incompatible with a business

options.text: Operator A is the business because it buys a recurring service and monetises access repeatedly
Operator B is the business because it holds the raw material, which is the asset that matters most
options.misconception: equates holding raw data with running an operation

questions.explanation: The brief's test is repeat monetisation of a bought service, which only Operator A shows. One-shot use of stolen credentials sells an asset rather than running a business, and renting access does not disqualify either side.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how staged disclosure serves an activist objective
questions.stem: The design brief weighs an activist campaign's two stages, staging a slow leak first and a public release later; which two-part description best captures the campaign's objective?

options.text: Stage one builds a credible record, and stage two converts that record into pressure on a decision-maker
Stage one rents access cheaply, and stage two sells the collected material to pay for it
options.misconception: recasts advocacy as resale for profit

options.misconception: reads staging as concealment rather than sequencing

options.misconception: conflates advocacy with state collection

questions.explanation: An activist campaign wants decisions to move in its favour, so staged leaks supply credible evidence and a release supplies pressure. The alternatives reduce it to resale, hiding or state collection.

questions.stem: The design brief assesses a contractor who can export a customer database on their last day; which statement captures the insider's real advantage?

options.text: They hold trusted access to the exact systems that matter, so misuse needs no technical trick

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a supply-chain compromise travels so far
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how downstream builds multiply a compromise
questions.stem: The design brief logs a compromised package that reached 240 downstream repositories within 2 hours; which reading of the spread best fits the brief?

options.text: Each repository was targeted separately, so the attacker ran 240 parallel intrusions
options.misconception: misreads replication as parallel targeting

options.text: Each build that consumed the package re-published it, so reach multiplied with every downstream build
The package registry pushed the update to all subscribers, which is a distribution feature
options.misconception: treats the registry as the spreading mechanism

options.text: The developers copied the package by hand into each repository to speed up the rollout
options.misconception: invents manual copying as the mechanism

questions.explanation: Downstream builds re-publish what they consume, so each consumer adds a distribution point and the total climbs fast. Separate intrusions, a registry push and manual copying are different mechanisms.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why the target's own site is useful to an attacker
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value an attacker draws from reconnaissance
questions.stem: The design brief asks why an attacker spends time on the target's public web presence when direct access is available; explain the value that reconnaissance provides.

answer.exemplar: Reconnaissance converts a guess into a targeted approach. The public site reveals who holds which role, which suppliers and partners are named, which pages and file types are exposed, and which services the organisation advertises. Those facts let an attacker choose a plausible pretext and a likely entry point instead of testing indiscriminately. The site also serves as a trusted distribution point for payloads aimed at the organisation's own users, so the same reconnaissance supports both entry and delivery.

questions.explanation: Reconnaissance narrows the attack by identifying people, suppliers, entry points and delivery channels. Without it the attacker pays for blind trials, which is why the target's own site is worth the time.

questions.topic: The dilemma a zero-day finder faces
questions.learningObjective: Compute remaining exposure at a chosen publication date
questions.stem: The design brief lets a researcher publish 90 days after discovery; if a vendor needs 45 days to ship a fix and 14 days for validation, how many days of user exposure remain at publication?
questions.explanation: Fix plus validation takes 45 plus 14, which is 59 days, so publishing on day 90 leaves 31 days of exposure. Comparing 90 with only the fix time would overstate the window by the validation period.

options.text: The first operator is a criminal crew and the second is a state actor, judged by the length of the stay
options.misconception: uses dwell time alone to classify an operator

options.text: The first operator is a state actor and the second is criminal, judged by the lack of any data sale
options.misconception: infers motive from absence of a single behaviour

options.text: The first operator wants intelligence and the second wants profit, judged by what was taken and done

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a state-aligned campaign tolerates a long stay inside
questions.learningObjective: Compare how quiet and fast disclosure affect users
questions.stem: The design brief considers an operator that stays quiet so a vendor can patch and another that publishes immediately; which two-part reading best describes how each affects users?

options.text: The quiet operator protects users because patches always arrive first, while the quick operator exposes them
options.misconception: treats silence as a guarantee of a fix

options.text: The quiet operator delays the fix because vendors use the time to prepare a counter-move
options.misconception: invents vendor retaliation as the reason

options.text: Both operators produce the same result, since disclosure timing does not change user risk
options.misconception: denies any effect of timing on exposure

options.text: The quiet operator may reduce exposure if the patch lands, while the quick operator reduces it sooner but with less testing

questions.explanation: Private disclosure trades certainty of a fix for a window where only the vendor knows; publication shrinks that window but shortens testing. Neither route removes exposure alone.

questions.learningObjective: Separate an established criminal operation from opportunistic crime
questions.stem: The design brief asks which feature most clearly separates a criminal operation run like a firm from opportunistic individual crime; which option fits?

options.text: The crew can be hired by an unrelated party to carry out an attack
options.misconception: assumes service hiring marks criminal enterprise

options.text: The crew recruits members through a forum that also hosts unrelated criminal activity
options.misconception: treats a shared forum as proof of firm structure

options.text: The crew is located in one country and targets systems in a second country
options.misconception: treats geography as the marker of an organisation

options.text: The crew retains and reuses access over time, expecting it to generate further revenue

questions.explanation: Reusing retained access for future revenue shows continuity and planning, which one-off opportunists lack. Hiring services, forum presence and cross-border targeting all occur in opportunistic crime too.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an activist campaign is optimising for
questions.learningObjective: Compare concentrated reach with sustained reach
questions.stem: The design brief compares a leak that reached 3000 readers in one day with a campaign that reached 200 readers daily for a month; which conclusion does the brief support?

options.text: The single-day leak was less effective because reaching many people once cannot change behaviour
options.misconception: assumes scale without repetition has no effect

options.text: The month-long campaign was less effective because 200 daily readers is a trivial audience
options.misconception: judges impact by audience size alone

options.text: The two differ in shape: one concentrates attention briefly, the other sustains it
The two are equivalent because 3000 readers roughly equals 200 readers over 15 days
options.misconception: conflates a one-off spike with a sustained run

questions.explanation: A single spike concentrates attention briefly while a sustained run keeps the issue present; the brief treats them as different shapes of reach. Comparing raw totals hides that distinction.
questions.hint: Shape of reach, not raw totals.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The asymmetry an insider holds
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish departing insiders from malicious insiders
questions.stem: The design brief asks why departing staff create a different insider risk from malicious insiders; explain the distinction the brief draws.

answer.exemplar: A departing employee is not necessarily hostile, but the access they hold stops being justified the moment they leave. Their credentials, tokens and shared accounts often remain live because offboarding is incomplete, and the brief treats that gap as the real risk rather than intent. A malicious insider acts deliberately from inside; a departing insider is an unclosed account with legitimate history, which makes detection depend on lifecycle hygiene instead of behavioural suspicion.

questions.explanation: The brief separates intent from exposure: a departing insider means unclosed access, a malicious insider plans from inside. Detection differs too, resting on offboarding hygiene versus behaviour.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes criminal operations a business
questions.learningObjective: Identify the conditions that make intrusion work repeatable
questions.stem: The design brief asks what makes criminal intrusion work repeatable; explain the three conditions the brief treats as necessary.

answer.exemplar: Three conditions make the work repeatable. The crew needs a supplier of initial access it can rely on, so one compromised partner does not have to be found each time. It needs a method for turning access into value that does not depend on the target noticing, which is why quiet collection or resale is preferred over noisy disruption. Finally it needs somewhere to sell or use what it takes, so the loop closes and the same effort can be repeated against the next target.

questions.explanation: The brief names dependable access, a repeatable route from access to value and a market for the result as the conditions that let the loop close. Without a buyer, effort stops instead of repeating.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a supply-chain compromise travels so far
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a stolen build agent reaches customer devices
questions.stem: The design brief considers a compromised build agent and the software it signs; which two-part chain explains how the compromise reaches customer devices?

options.text: The agent is stolen, then the stolen signing key is published so customers distrust the vendor
options.misconception: invents key publication as the delivery step

options.text: The agent is stolen, then the vendor's public keys are rotated to remove the malicious build
options.misconception: reverses the trust relationship in the chain

options.text: The agent is stolen, then customers who verify signatures still install the tampered artefact
options.misconception: claims verification fails against a valid signature

options.text: The agent is stolen, then the trusted build signs a tampered artefact that passes verification

questions.explanation: The chain runs through trust, not around it: a stolen signing agent produces a tampered artefact with a genuine signature, so verification passes. Rotation or key publication would not carry the compromise to users.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching an actor category to what it wants
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish espionage and criminal operators during triage
questions.stem: The design brief asks how an engineer should tell an espionage operator apart from a criminal one during triage; explain the distinguishing evidence.

answer.exemplar: Triage should compare what the operator took with what they did afterwards. An espionage operator leaves the environment largely intact, keeps access for later collection and rarely monetises anything, so the footprint is access and observation rather than extraction. A criminal operator moves data out and converts it, often through resale, and shows little interest in the target afterwards. Where both behaviours appear, the deciding evidence is persistence of access alongside no cash-out, which points away from resale and towards collection.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing evidence is what happened to the data and whether access persisted. Keeping access without monetising points to collection; extraction plus resale points to crime. Intent is inferred from behaviour.

options.misconception: ignores the first hop of the chain

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why the target's own site is useful to an attacker
questions.learningObjective: Explain how public technology choices become attack surface
questions.stem: The design brief asks why a target's public technology choices matter to an attacker; explain how a stack choice becomes an attack surface.

answer.exemplar: Public technology choices narrow the attacker's search. When a site advertises a particular content platform, mail service or version banner, the attacker can search for known flaws in exactly that product and prepare a matching payload instead of testing broadly. The same disclosure also reveals which integrations are trusted, for example a single sign-on provider, and where a stolen session might be accepted. The stack is therefore both a map of likely weaknesses and a list of the boundaries where a stolen credential can be replayed.

questions.explanation: Knowing the stack lets an attacker match known flaws and target the integrations where replay works, rather than guessing. The stack is both a weakness map and a map of where a stolen session is accepted.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The asymmetry an insider holds
questions.learningObjective: Explain why outsider controls miss insider activity
questions.stem: The design brief asks why insider risk is hard to detect with the controls built for outsiders; explain the mismatch.

answer.exemplar: Controls built for outsiders assume the attacker must cross a boundary, so the system watches for a blocked attempt, a failed sign-in or a novel privilege use. An insider needs none of that: they authenticate correctly, arrive through approved channels and use permissions that were granted to them. Their activity therefore matches an expected pattern, and the signals that would raise a flag for an outsider never fire. Detection therefore depends on lifecycle and behaviour review rather than perimeter events.

questions.explanation: Outsider detection relies on boundary events, but insider activity is authenticated and approved, so those signals never fire. That is why the brief points to lifecycle review and behaviour baselines.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What makes criminal operations a business
questions.learningObjective: Explain why criminal operators resist changing their tooling
questions.stem: The design brief asks why criminal operators resist change to their tooling; explain what the brief says about the risk of replacing a working tool.

answer.exemplar: The brief argues that a working tool is a known quantity. Its operational habits are understood, its failure modes are known and its suppliers are established, so the operator can predict what a given run will produce. Swapping it introduces unknowns: new behaviour to learn, new infrastructure to build, new contacts to trust and a fresh trail for defenders to notice. Any gain from a new tool has to outweigh that whole learning cost, which is why the crew keeps a tool that works.

questions.explanation: A working tool carries known behaviour and a tested supply chain; switching brings learning cost, new trails and new trust. That asymmetry, not loyalty, explains why crews resist change.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Matching an actor category to what it wants
questions.learningObjective: Define an actor category so it remains useful
questions.stem: The design brief asks why the same category name can cover behaviour that looks very different; explain how a category is defined so it stays useful.

answer.exemplar: A category is useful only if it is defined by the objective rather than by the technique. If the label is built from how an operator gets in, then a state operator using ordinary stolen passwords and a criminal crew using a custom implant both look like credential thieves, and their targets and tolerances become impossible to compare. Defined by what they are trying to achieve, the same two cases separate cleanly: one wants lasting access and intelligence, the other wants cash and quick extraction, with different dwell times and different evidence trails.

questions.explanation: Categories built on technique collapse when one technique serves different aims, so the brief defines each by objective. Technique-based labels hide the differences in dwell and evidence that drive response.
